note: Considers how people change behaviour in response to a model, which means fairness at the prediction alone is not enough.
title: Strategic Best-Response Fairness Framework for Fair Machine Learning
explain_beginner: Machine learning systems often make decisions about people, like who gets a loan or a job. Usually, fairness is checked only by looking at the predictions themselves. This paper says that is not enough, because people change their behavior based on those predictions. For example, if a system seems biased, people might give up trying. The authors introduce a new idea called strategic best-response fairness. It asks whether two groups that start out the same end up putting in the same effort and getting the same results. They found that many common fairness methods do not achieve this, but one method, equalized odds, does, though it has practical problems. The paper argues that fairness must consider how people react, not just the prediction.
explain_business: This research shows that fair predictions alone may not prevent discrimination. People change their behavior based on how algorithms treat them, so a model that looks fair can still lead to unequal effort and outcomes. The paper introduces strategic best-response fairness, which checks whether groups that start out identical end up with the same behavior and results. It finds that common fairness methods like demographic parity do not guarantee this, while equalized odds does but with practical drawbacks. For executives, this means fairness audits should include behavioral responses, not just prediction metrics. Decisions about deploying ML should consider whether the system encourages equal effort and outcomes across groups, and may require designing algorithms specifically for this goal.
explain_practitioner: The paper proposes strategic best-response fairness (SBR-fairness) as a framework for fair machine learning. It moves beyond fairness in prediction alone, arguing that individuals may alter their behavior in response to algorithmic decisions. The key question is whether an algorithm trained on potentially biased data leads to identical equilibrium behaviors across subpopulations that are ex ante identical. The authors evaluate common fair-ML algorithms. They find that color-blindness and demographic parity criteria do not always achieve SBR fairness, meaning disparities in effort and outcomes can persist. Equalized odds does achieve SBR fairness, but it has several practical limitations. The work suggests SBR fairness is a necessary condition for breaking discrimination cycles and offers a complementary assessment tool.
